1. The animation shows how US consumer prices (CPI-U) have moved against a "first check", such as the first payment from a fixed income stream. It uses US history from 1947 to August 2006. It is labeled "illustrative", "history, not a forecast", and "US only".

2. The bar chart is the same in all six frames. What changes is the overlay. Frame 1 shows only the first check (the green bar) and a top reference line labeled "80.…". Frame 2 adds a second line labeled "54.…" and the text "typical level check: 54.3%, about half". Frame 4 has the same content, with a slightly different layout. Frame 5 adds "level check there by about year 8" and a segmented progress bar. Frame 6 adds the note "Each check vs its own first check · not dollars."

3. The chart appears to measure how each later check compares with that first check, in relative terms rather than dollar amounts. The bars start high, fall to a long trough, then climb back toward the 80 line. The typical reading is about 54.3%, roughly half. The "year 8" label seems to say a check typically reaches that halfway level within about eight years. I'm not certain of that, because the axis labels are cut off ("80.:", "54.:") and the chart doesn't say what is being measured.

4. A viewer would take no explicit advice from this. The animation doesn't tell anyone to choose or avoid a payout option. It only presents a historical pattern and says it isn't a forecast.

5. None.
